Sign in as the root user, open Security credentials and assign an MFA device (passkey, security key or authenticator app). Keep the device and the recovery details in a safe place that more than one admin can reach. The resource id has unsupported characters and is shown with ? in their place. |
| `prowler` | `iam_user_mfa_enabled_console_access` | `nr-console-user` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(j), NIS2 Art.21(2)(i), DORA Art.9, DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art.21, NIS2 CIR 2024/2690 Annex 11.7, ISO27001:2022 A.8.5 |  | guidance only | No code is generated: an MFA device belongs to the person who holds it, so each user adds it. Find users with a console password and no MFA: aws iam generate-credential-report, then aws iam get-credential-report (columns password_enabled and mfa_active). Ask each user to assign an MFA device under Security credentials. If a user does not need the console, remove the password: aws iam delete-login-profile --user-name USER. A policy that denies actions without aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent can enforce MFA, but test it on one user first, or users are locked out. |

Move any use to an IAM role. Then sign in as the root user, open Security credentials, deactivate the keys, wait to see that nothing breaks, and delete them. The resource id has unsupported characters and is shown with ? in their place. |

Turn on validation: aws cloudtrail update-trail --name TRAIL --enable-log-file-validation. | `prowler` | `cloudtrail_kms_encryption_enabled` | `nr-trail` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(h), DORA Art.9, DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art.6, NIS2 CIR 2024/2690 Annex 9.1, ISO27001:2022 A.8.24 |  | guidance only | No code is generated because the trail and the key policy are not in your Terraform state. Use a symmetric customer-managed KMS key in the region of the trail bucket. Its key policy must let cloudtrail.amazonaws.com use kms:GenerateDataKey\* and let log readers use kms:Decrypt. Then run: aws cloudtrail update-trail --name TRAIL --kms-key-id KEY_ARN. A wrong key policy stops log delivery, so check aws cloudtrail get-trail-status --name TRAIL after the change. Log files written before the change keep their old encryption. |

If the cluster is in your Terraform code, set enabled_cluster_log_types on aws_eks_cluster instead. | `prowler` | `eks_cluster_kms_cmk_encryption_in_secrets_enabled` | `nr-eks` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(h), DORA Art.9, DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art.6, NIS2 CIR 2024/2690 Annex 9.1, ISO27001:2022 A.8.24 |  | guidance only | No safe drop-in code exists because the cluster is not in your Terraform state. Secrets encryption cannot be turned off once it is on, and if the key is disabled or deleted the cluster cannot read its secrets. Use a symmetric customer-managed KMS key in the cluster region and keep it from being deleted. Then run: aws eks associate-encryption-config --cluster-name CLUSTER --encryption-config '\[{"resources":\["secrets"\],"provider":{"keyArn":"KEY_ARN"}}\]'. When the update is done, rewrite the existing secrets so they are encrypted with the key: kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json \| kubectl annotate --overwrite -f - kms-encryption-timestamp=TIME. |

| `prowler` | `ec2_securitygroup_default_restrict_traffic` | `sg-0123456789abcdef0` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(i), NIS2 Art.21(2)(g), DORA Art.9, DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art.13, NIS2 CIR 2024/2690 Annex 6.7, ISO27001:2022 A.8.20, ISO27001:2022 A.8.22 |  | guidance only | No code is generated on purpose. Removing the rules of a default security group cuts off every instance or interface that still uses it. Find them: aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters Name=group-id,Values=SG. Move them to their own security groups. Then list the rules (aws ec2 describe-security-group-rules --filters Name=group-id,Values=SG) and remove each one with aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress or aws ec2 revoke-security-group-egress --group-id SG --security-group-rule-ids RULE. The default group itself cannot be deleted. |
